stages.title: Drawing techniques
stages.hook: How could you make one pencil give you light grey, dark grey and black? Test it on scrap paper.
explain: Artists use different marks to make drawings. Hatching is a set of parallel lines. Cross-hatching adds a second set that crosses the first, which makes the area darker. Stippling uses tiny dots: more dots close together make a darker area.
A contour line follows the edge of a shape. Gesture drawing uses quick, loose lines to catch the movement of a subject. Blending smooths pencil marks with a finger or paper stump.
Pencils have grades. H pencils are hard and make pale lines. B pencils are soft and make dark lines. HB is in the middle. Press lightly first, then darker, so you can fix mistakes.

example.q: You want a dark patch with only an HB pencil. Which technique could you use?
steps: Choose a mark: hatching, cross-hatching or stippling.
Cross-hatching layers lines in two directions.
Add a third layer if it is still pale.
The crossing lines make the area darker.
example.a: Cross-hatching, adding more layers until dark enough

analogies.home: Hatching is like the lines in a woven mat: more layers, thicker look.
analogies.nature: Dots can show the speckles on a bird egg, stippling style.
analogies.sport: A gesture sketch of a runner uses fast lines, like a sprint.
analogies.tech: A screen picture is made of tiny dots, a bit like stippling.

stages.mnemonic: H is hard and high up pale; B is black and bold.
terms: Parallel lines used to build tone.
Two sets of crossing lines that make darker tone.
A line that follows the edge or surface of a form.

misc.wrong: Pressing very hard gives the best drawing.
misc.right: Good drawings start with light lines and build darkness slowly, so you can correct them.

stages.limits: Pencil grade labels differ slightly between brands, so test your pencils.

trip.prompt: Find a hatched or cross-hatched drawing. Which parts look darkest?

questions.q: Which technique uses dots to make tone?
questions.why: Stippling builds tone from dots.

questions.q: What does cross-hatching do compared with hatching?
o: Makes areas darker with crossing layers
Makes areas lighter by lifting lines away
Removes every line from the drawing
Draws only outlines with no tone at all
questions.why: The second layer of lines crossing the first adds darkness.

questions.q: Which pencil makes the darkest line?
questions.why: B grades are soft and dark. Higher B numbers are darker.

questions.q: What is gesture drawing mainly for?
o: Measuring with a ruler and pencil
questions.why: Gesture drawings are quick and show motion.

questions.q: You are drawing a fluffy dandelion seed head with tiny parts. Which technique suits it?
questions.why: Little dots show soft, light textures.

questions.q: Match the technique to what it does.
questions.why: Each technique makes a different kind of mark.

questions.q: Why start with light pressure?
o: You can fix mistakes and add darks later
Light pencil is cheaper than dark pencil
questions.why: Light lines are easy to rub out and darken.

questions.q: A learner gets a smudged drawing by rubbing it with a hand. What could help?
o: Rub the drawing harder so the graphite settles into the paper
Lay a thin damp cloth over the drawing while you work on it
Spray water on the drawing to fix the graphite in place
Use a clean paper stump or keep a spare sheet under the hand
questions.why: A clean barrier stops graphite smearing.

questions.q: Explain how cross-hatching makes a darker area than hatching.
questions.model: In cross-hatching a second set of lines crosses the first, so there are more lines and less white paper showing, making the area look darker.
questions.why: More marks and less white paper make a darker tone.

questions.q: Why might an artist choose a quick gesture sketch before a final drawing?
o: To use up all the old pencils
To make the paper look dirty
To avoid looking at the model
questions.why: Gesture sketches help plan the energy and shape.

panel.q: Two drawings of a tree trunk look equally dark, one with hatching and one with stippling. What does this show?
o: Hatching never works for dark areas
Different marks can make similar tone
Stippling is always lighter than lines
Tone cannot be made with marks at all
panel.why: Tone depends on how much of the paper is covered, not only the kind of mark.

panel.q: If you want a smooth sky, which is better?
panel.why: Blending makes smooth, even tone.

panel.q: Why do artists use more than one pencil grade?
panel.model: A hard pencil gives pale, fine lines for planning and detail, while a soft pencil gives rich dark tones, so using both gives a wider range.
panel.why: Different grades give a range of tones.

teach.model: Artists make tone with marks. Hatching is lines, cross-hatching is lines crossing, and stippling is dots. More marks mean a darker area. Hard pencils (H) are pale and soft pencils (B) are dark.

points.ask: What kinds of marks are there?
How do I make an area darker?

stages.title: Proportion and composition
stages.hook: Cover half of a picture you like. Does it still feel balanced? Why or why not?
explain: Proportion means how big one part is compared with another. In a drawing of a person, the head is a useful measuring unit. Many drawing guides say adults are about seven to eight heads tall, while young children are fewer heads tall because their heads are larger for their bodies.

Composition means how you arrange things in a picture. A focal point is the place the eye goes first. The rule of thirds divides a picture into a 3 by 3 grid with two lines across and two down. Putting the focal point near where the lines cross often feels pleasing.

Artists also use balance, overlap and a foreground, middle ground and background. These are guidelines, not laws. Many artists in Japan, Africa and Europe have placed subjects in the centre or off to the side to make different feelings.

example.q: A rule of thirds grid has 2 lines across and 2 down. How many equal boxes does it make?
steps: Count the sections across: 3.
Count the sections down: 3.
Multiply: 3 × 3 = 9.
Check: 4 crossing points also appear.

analogies.home: Arranging furniture so a room feels balanced is a bit like composition.
analogies.city: A photographer places a tall tower off-centre to make a stronger photo.
analogies.sport: On a football pitch, players spread out to balance the field, like objects in a picture.
analogies.music: A song has a loud part and a soft part, like busy and empty areas in a picture.

stages.mnemonic: Thirds make nine, and the focus goes on a line.
terms: How things are arranged in a picture.
The place that draws the eye first.
The part of a scene closest to the viewer.

misc.wrong: The subject must always be exactly in the middle.
misc.right: A centred subject can look calm, but off-centre can make a more lively composition. It depends on what the artist wants.

stages.limits: Proportion guides like head-heights are averages. Real people vary, and some art stretches proportions on purpose.

trip.prompt: Look at the example photographs. Where is the main subject placed?

questions.q: How many equal boxes does a rule of thirds grid have?
questions.why: 3 across × 3 down = 9.

questions.q: How many places do the rule of thirds lines cross?
questions.why: Two horizontal and two vertical lines cross at 4 points.

questions.q: What is the focal point?
o: The frame around the whole picture, on all sides
The darkest corner of the page
The place the eye is drawn to first
questions.why: A focal point is the main point of interest.

questions.q: What does proportion describe?
o: Which colours are used in the whole picture
How big parts are compared with each other
questions.why: Proportion is about relative size.

questions.q: In a picture, which part is closest to the viewer?
questions.why: The foreground is nearest the viewer.

questions.q: An adult is drawn 7 heads tall. The head is 4 cm tall. How tall is the whole figure?
Your child figure looks adult-like. A good fix is to...
o: Make the head smaller compared with the body
Remove the arms so the body looks shorter
Make the head larger compared with the body
questions.why: Young children have larger heads in proportion to their bodies.

questions.q: A picture has a big empty area on the left and a crowded right. What might help balance it?
o: Remove some of the objects on the right until the picture is empty
Rotate the paper so the empty area is at the bottom
Add something on the left or move the main subject
Colour everything on the right black to match the left
questions.why: Balance spreads visual weight.

questions.q: Explain why artists sometimes break the rule of thirds.
questions.model: The rule of thirds is only a guide. A central subject can feel calm or powerful, so artists choose it on purpose.
questions.why: Guidelines serve the artist's intention.

questions.q: A tall thin canvas could suit which subject best?
questions.why: The canvas shape can echo the subject.

panel.q: Two students draw the same bowl. One places it in the corner, the other in the centre. Who is right?
o: Both can be, depending on the effect they want
Only the corner, because off-centre is always right
Only the centre, because the rule of thirds is a law
Neither, because compositions cannot be judged
panel.why: Composition choices are about effect, not one right answer.

panel.q: Why is overlapping a good way to show depth?
o: It uses much less paper than other methods do
It makes all the colours brighter
The front object hides part of the back object
panel.why: Overlap shows which things are in front.

panel.q: A drawing looks flat and crowded. Suggest one change to its composition.
panel.model: I would remove some small objects, make the main one bigger as the focal point, and overlap others so there is a clear foreground and background.
panel.why: Clear focus and depth cues fix crowded compositions.

teach.model: Proportion is how big parts are compared to each other. Composition is how you arrange things in a picture. A focal point is where the eye goes first. The rule of thirds divides a picture into nine boxes.

points.ask: What is the rule of thirds?

stages.title: Perspective fundamentals
stages.hook: Stand by a long straight road or corridor. Why does it look as if the sides meet far away?
explain: Perspective is a way to show depth on a flat surface. Far things look smaller and higher on the page, and near things look bigger and lower. Overlap also shows depth: a thing in front hides part of what is behind.

In one-point perspective, parallel lines going away from you seem to meet at one spot called the vanishing point. It sits on the horizon line, which is at your eye level. Lines that run straight across stay horizontal, and tall lines stay vertical.

The Italian architect Filippo Brunelleschi demonstrated linear perspective in Florence in the early 1400s, and it spread in European art. Other traditions, such as many Chinese scroll paintings and Japanese woodblock prints, show depth with different methods like stacked layers and mist, and they are not worse or better.

example.q: Draw a road leading to the horizon. Where do the road edges meet?
steps: Draw a horizontal horizon line at eye level.
Mark a vanishing point on the line.
Draw the road edges from near the bottom to that point.
The edges meet at the vanishing point.
example.a: At the vanishing point on the horizon line

analogies.city: Tall buildings along a street look as if their rooflines slope to a distant point.
analogies.farm: Fence posts along a field look smaller the further away they are.
analogies.sea: Waves near a boat look bigger than waves near the horizon.
analogies.nature: Rows of trees in a forest path get smaller, then meet in the distance.

stages.mnemonic: Eye level is the horizon, and lines run home to the vanishing point.
terms: A way to show depth on a flat surface.
The line at eye level where sky and ground seem to meet.
The spot where parallel lines seem to meet.
When a front object covers part of one behind it.

misc.wrong: Perspective only exists in European art.
misc.right: Many cultures show depth, using different tools such as overlap, layers and scale. Linear perspective is one method.

stages.limits: Linear perspective is a simplification of how eyes and brains see depth.

trip.prompt: Find a picture with a vanishing point. Where is the horizon line?

questions.q: What is the vanishing point?
o: A hole in the corner of the paper
The darkest spot in a picture
Where parallel lines seem to meet
The place where the paper ends
questions.why: In perspective drawing, parallel lines going away meet at a vanishing point.

questions.q: Where is the vanishing point in one-point perspective?
o: At the bottom of the page
questions.why: It sits on the horizon line at eye level.

questions.q: Which looks farther away in a picture?
o: A smaller object higher on the page
A bigger object lower down on the page
questions.why: Distance is shown by smaller size and higher placement.

questions.q: What does overlap show?
questions.why: The overlapping object is in front.

questions.q: Two railway tracks go away from you. How do they appear?
o: They seem to come closer together
They stay the same distance on the page
questions.why: Parallel lines appear to converge in the distance.

questions.q: The horizon line is placed very low. What does the picture show?
questions.why: A low horizon leaves more room for the sky.

questions.q: Match the term to its meaning.
questions.why: These are key perspective words.

questions.q: Order the steps to draw a one-point perspective road.
items: Draw the road edges to that point
questions.why: Set the framework first, then add objects.

questions.q: Explain why railway tracks seem to meet in a drawing even though they stay the same distance apart.
questions.model: Tracks stay the same distance apart, but far parts look smaller, so lines seem to come together at a vanishing point.
questions.why: Perspective is how distance changes what we see.

questions.q: A friend says a scroll painting with mist and stacked mountains is wrong because it has no vanishing point. What is the best reply?
o: It uses a different way of showing depth
They are right, so the painting is wrong
Mist is a mistake that spoils paintings
Mountains cannot be stacked in a picture
questions.why: Chinese landscape painting shows depth with layers and atmosphere.

panel.q: If you move your eye level higher, what happens to the horizon line in your drawing?
o: It moves lower down the page
panel.why: The horizon is always at your eye level.

panel.q: Why do vertical walls stay vertical in simple one-point perspective?
o: Walls cannot move in a drawing
Verticals vanish at a third point on the horizon
Only lines going away converge in that method
The paper is flat so lines stay vertical
panel.why: In one-point perspective, lines parallel to the picture plane stay parallel.

panel.q: How could you show a path going far away without using a vanishing point?
panel.model: Draw faraway things smaller and higher, overlap them, and make them paler like mist, so distance is clear.
panel.why: Depth cues other than linear perspective are valid.

teach.model: Perspective shows depth on flat paper. Far things look small. Lines going away meet at a vanishing point on the horizon line. Overlap also shows what is in front.

stages.title: Colour theory
stages.hook: Look at the colour wheel. Which colour is across from red, and why might artists put them side by side?
explain: The colour wheel arranges colours in a circle. It has three primary colours (red, yellow, blue), three secondary colours (orange, green, purple) and six tertiary colours made by mixing a primary with a neighbouring secondary. That makes twelve in all.

Colours opposite each other on the wheel are complementary: red and green, blue and orange, yellow and purple. Side by side they look very strong. Colours next to each other are analogous and look harmonious, like blue, blue-green and green.

A tint is a colour plus white, a shade is a colour plus black, and a tone is a colour plus grey. Artists in every culture use colour to carry meaning, but meanings differ: white is worn for celebration in some places and mourning in others.

example.q: Which colour is complementary to blue on the traditional painter's wheel?
steps: Find blue on the wheel.
Look straight across the circle.
You reach orange.
So blue and orange are complementary.

analogies.home: A blue cup on an orange tablecloth stands out.
analogies.nature: Orange poppies against green leaves pop because they are near opposites.
analogies.sport: Team shirts often use contrasting colours so players can be told apart.
analogies.city: Warning signs use strong colour pairs so they are easy to see.

stages.mnemonic: Opposites attract: across the wheel, complements.
terms: Colours opposite each other on the colour wheel.
Colours next to each other on the wheel.
A mix of a primary and a neighbouring secondary.

misc.wrong: Colour meanings are the same everywhere.
misc.right: Colours carry different meanings in different cultures, so artists check the context.

stages.limits: The red-yellow-blue wheel is a teaching tool. Light and printing use other primary sets.

trip.prompt: Spin through the colour wheel page. Can you find three pairs of complements?

questions.q: How many colours are on a standard twelve-part wheel?
questions.why: 3 primary + 3 secondary + 6 tertiary = 12.

questions.q: Which pair is complementary?
questions.why: Yellow and purple sit opposite each other on the wheel.

questions.q: Which set of colours is analogous?
o: Orange and blue, side by side
questions.why: Analogous colours sit next to each other.

questions.q: What is a tint?
questions.why: Tint means lighter by adding white.

questions.q: What do you add to make a shade?
questions.why: A shade is darker by adding black.

questions.q: You paint a red apple and want it to stand out in the picture. Which background helps?
questions.why: Complementary contrast makes the apple pop.

questions.q: To paint a calm sea picture, which colour plan fits best?
o: Red and green with hot orange
Orange and blue in equal parts
Black and red with some yellow
questions.why: Analogous cool colours feel calm.

questions.q: Match each colour to its complement.
questions.why: These are the traditional complementary pairs.

questions.q: Why might an artist put complementary colours side by side?
questions.model: Complementary colours are opposites, so side by side they contrast strongly and make each other look brighter.
questions.why: Opposites on the wheel create strong contrast.

questions.q: A mix of equal amounts of red and green paint often looks...
questions.why: Complements mix toward muted brown or grey.

panel.q: A student says "red always means danger". What is the best response?
o: They are always right, because red means danger everywhere
Red has no meaning in any culture
Meanings change with culture and context
panel.why: Colour meanings vary around the world.

panel.q: Why might an artist add a little of the complementary colour to a mix?
o: To make it glow much brighter
To mute and dull the colour
To make it vanish from the picture
panel.why: Adding the opposite lowers intensity.

panel.q: Describe how to make a pale blue for a morning sky.
panel.model: Mix a small amount of blue into white to make a pale tint of blue.
panel.why: A tint is made by adding white.

teach.model: The colour wheel shows twelve colours. Colours opposite each other are complementary. Colours next to each other are analogous. White makes a tint and black makes a shade.

points.ask: How do I make lighter or darker colours?

stages.title: Shading and tonal values
stages.hook: Squint at a photo of a sphere. Where do you see the lightest and darkest areas?
explain: Value (or tone) means how light or dark something is. A value scale goes from white through greys to black. Using many values makes a drawing look three-dimensional.

When light hits a round object, there is a highlight where light hits most, a light area, a midtone, a core shadow (the darkest area on the object), reflected light along the edge, and a cast shadow on the surface behind. The cast shadow is the darkest shadow near the object.

Shade by building layers gently. Move the pencil in the shape of the form, for example curved lines on a ball. Cultures around the world used light and dark: Renaissance painters in Italy called strong light–dark contrast chiaroscuro, and shadow plays in Indonesia use shadow as art itself.

example.q: A lamp is above-left of a ball. Where is the cast shadow?
steps: Find the light direction: above-left.
Light travels toward the lower right.
The ball blocks light.
The cast shadow falls to the lower right of the ball.
example.a: On the table to the lower right of the ball

analogies.home: A mug by a window has a bright side and a dark side.
analogies.nature: A boulder in the sun has a sunny side and a shaded side.
analogies.music: Loud and soft parts of music are like light and dark values.
analogies.tech: A black-and-white photo shows only value, no colour.

stages.mnemonic: Highlight, light, mid, core, cast: five steps from bright to last.
terms: How light or dark a tone is.
The brightest area where light hits.
The darkest part on the object itself.
The shadow an object throws on a surface.

misc.wrong: A shadow is just one flat grey patch.
misc.right: A shadow has varying values, darker near the object and with reflected light inside.

stages.limits: Real lighting can be complicated with many light sources. Simple lessons use one light.

trip.prompt: Find paintings with strong light and dark. Where is the light coming from?

questions.q: What is value in art?
o: How light or dark something is
How warm or cool something looks
How much it costs to buy
How big it is on the whole page
questions.why: Value means lightness or darkness.

questions.q: Where is the highlight on a ball lit from the top?
questions.why: The highlight is where the light hits most directly.

questions.q: What is the darkest part on the ball itself called?
questions.why: The core shadow is the darkest region on the object.

questions.q: What is a cast shadow?
o: The bright spot on top of an object
A shadow thrown onto another surface
questions.why: It is cast by the object onto the surface.

questions.q: How do you shade a ball so it looks round?
o: Use curved strokes following its shape
Use straight lines only, side to side
questions.why: Curved strokes follow the form.

questions.q: A lamp is on the right. The cast shadow is on the...
questions.why: Shadows are on the opposite side of the light.

questions.q: Order from lightest to darkest on a lit ball.
questions.why: Value goes down from highlight to core shadow.

questions.q: Match the word to what it is.
pairs: Light bouncing back at the edge
questions.why: These are parts of shading a form.

questions.q: Explain why using many values makes a drawing look three-dimensional.
questions.model: Different values show how light falls across a form, so light and dark areas suggest that it is round and solid rather than flat.
questions.why: Gradual value changes describe form.

questions.q: Why are black and white photos still useful to artists?
o: They show colour better than paint
questions.why: Value is easier to see without colour.

panel.q: A ball drawing has a perfect grey fill. What is the problem?
o: It has far too many different values in it
It has no value change, so it looks flat
panel.why: Variation in value makes a form.

panel.q: Why add reflected light on the shadow side?
o: Light bounces off nearby surfaces and softens the shadow
To make it brighter than the highlight itself
panel.why: Reflected light keeps the shadow side from being flat black.

panel.q: How does the position of a light source change a drawing?
panel.model: The light decides where the highlight is and which side the shadow falls on; low light makes longer shadows.
panel.why: Light direction controls light and shadow positions.

teach.model: Value means how light or dark something is. A round object has a highlight, midtone, core shadow and cast shadow. Shading with changing values makes a drawing look solid.

points.ask: What are the parts of shading?

stages.title: Watercolour painting
stages.hook: What happens when you touch a wet brush of colour onto wet paper? Try it and watch the paint spread.
explain: Watercolour is paint made of pigment mixed with a water-soluble binder. It is transparent, so light passes through it and bounces off the paper. This is why painters usually keep white areas by leaving the paper unpainted, instead of using white paint.

In a wash you spread a thin, even layer of colour. In wet-on-wet you add colour to a damp surface so it blooms and softens. In wet-on-dry you paint onto dry paper for crisp edges. Most painters work from light to dark because it is hard to make a dark colour pale again.

Watercolour is used around the world. Albrecht Dürer made famous watercolour landscapes in Germany around 1500, and Chinese and Japanese painters use ink washes with water and brush skills. Use thick paper meant for watercolour so it does not buckle.

example.q: You want a pale yellow sun with a bright white cloud. How do you keep the cloud white?
steps: Plan the cloud shape first.
Paint the sky around the cloud.
Leave the cloud as bare paper.
The paper itself gives the white.

analogies.home: Tea staining on paper is like a pale wash.
analogies.nature: Rain on a window makes colours run, a bit like wet-on-wet.
analogies.sea: A wash of blue fading to white looks like shallow water.
analogies.farm: Wet-on-wet suits soft clouds above a field.

stages.mnemonic: Light first, dark last; keep the white for the paper.
terms: A thin, even layer of watercolour.
Painting onto damp paper so colours blend and soften.
Painting onto dry paper for sharp edges.

misc.wrong: Use white paint for the lightest areas in watercolour.
misc.right: Traditional watercolourists save the white of the paper, because the paint is transparent.

stages.limits: Some artists use white gouache or masking fluid; the rules are flexible.

trip.prompt: Find watercolours. Where did the artist leave the paper unpainted?

questions.q: Why is watercolour called transparent?
o: It has no colour of its own at all
It is made of clear glass
Light passes through it to the paper
questions.why: Transparency means light goes through the paint layer.

questions.q: How do traditional painters make white areas in watercolour?

questions.why: The paper provides the white.

questions.q: What is wet-on-wet?
o: Paint put on dry paper with a dry brush
Paint on damp paper so colours blend
questions.why: Wet-on-wet gives soft, flowing edges.

questions.q: What gives sharp edges?
questions.why: Paint on dry paper stays where you place it.

questions.q: Why paint light to dark?
o: Dark paint is too runny to control
Because black paint is not allowed
Dark paint is hard to lighten
questions.why: Transparent washes are hard to lift once dark.

questions.q: You want a soft, misty hill in the distance. Which method?
questions.why: Blurred edges look like mist.

questions.q: You want a crisp, sharp boat sail. Which method?
questions.why: Painting onto dry paper gives clear edges.

questions.q: Order a simple watercolour sky painting.
questions.why: Light first, details after it dries.

questions.q: Explain why thick watercolour paper is used.
questions.model: Thick paper can hold lots of water without wrinkling or buckling.
questions.why: Watercolour uses lots of water.

questions.q: Which artist painted watercolours around 1500 in Germany?
questions.why: Dürer made well-known watercolour landscapes about 1495 to 1500.

panel.q: Your painted dark mistake can't be fixed. What does this teach?
o: Never paint again after one mistake
Plan, and start with light colours
panel.why: Because it is transparent, you plan the lights first.

panel.q: A painter uses bold black ink lines and thin washes. What tradition might this resemble?
o: Cave painting from long ago only
panel.why: Ink and wash is a long tradition in China and Japan.

panel.q: Describe how to paint a pale sunset sky with soft colour mixing.
panel.model: Wet the paper, then drop in yellow, orange and pink so they blend softly in a wet-on-wet wash.
panel.why: Wet-on-wet blending is ideal for skies.

teach.model: Watercolour paint is see-through. You keep white areas by leaving the paper bare. Paint wet-on-wet for soft blends or wet-on-dry for sharp edges. Work from light to dark.

points.ask: What are the ways of painting?

stages.title: Acrylic painting
stages.hook: If paint dries in minutes and can be painted over, what new things could you do with it?
explain: Acrylic paint is made of pigment in an acrylic polymer binder. It is water-based while wet, dries fast, and becomes water-resistant when dry. You can use it thin like watercolour or thick like oil paint.

Because acrylic dries quickly, you can layer colours soon after. Mistakes can be painted over once dry. Wash brushes right away with water, or the paint will harden on them. Acrylics work on paper, card, wood, canvas and walls.

Commercial acrylic paints became popular for artists in the mid-1900s. In 1971, Aboriginal artists and community members at Papunya in central Australia began painting on boards and then canvas with acrylic paints, helping start a major movement in Indigenous Australian art.

example.q: Your sky is dry but you want to add white clouds on top. Can you?
steps: Check the layer is dry.
Pick a thick white acrylic.
Paint on top; it covers the layer below.
Dry acrylic does not dissolve.
example.a: Yes, paint opaque white over the dry blue

analogies.home: Craft paint on a wooden toy is often acrylic.
analogies.city: Many outdoor murals use acrylic or similar paints.
analogies.tech: Acrylic is a type of plastic-based paint.
analogies.nature: Painting a rock with acrylic makes a durable garden stone.

stages.mnemonic: Fast and flexible; wash it before it hardens.
terms: A fast-drying, water-based paint with a plastic binder.
Painting one dry layer over another.
A strong cloth stretched for painting.

misc.wrong: Acrylic never needs washing off brushes.
misc.right: Acrylic hardens and ruins brushes if left to dry, so wash them promptly.

trip.prompt: Look for pictures of acrylic paintings. Which look thin and which look thick?

questions.q: What is acrylic paint's binder?
questions.why: Acrylic uses a plastic-like polymer binder.

questions.q: How is acrylic paint cleaned while wet?
questions.why: Wet acrylic washes out with water.

questions.q: What happens to acrylic when it dries?
questions.why: Dry acrylic cannot be re-wetted.

questions.q: Acrylic compared with watercolour is usually...
questions.why: Acrylic can cover earlier layers when used thickly.

questions.q: Why can you paint over mistakes in acrylic?
o: It becomes invisible when it dries on top of another layer
It dries quickly and can cover earlier layers
It is made of rubber and stretches over mistakes
It stays wet forever so you can wipe it away
questions.why: Fast drying means quick layering.

questions.q: Your brush has dried hard. What went wrong?
o: Acrylic was not washed off in time
The paint was too bright and too thick
questions.why: Acrylic dries and hardens on brushes.

questions.q: If an artist waits 20 minutes between layers and applies 3 layers, how many minutes do they wait between them in total? Count waits between layers only.
questions.why: Between 3 layers there are 2 waits: 2 × 20 = 40.

questions.q: Match the term to its meaning.
questions.why: These are acrylic basics.

questions.q: Explain why acrylic is good for painting a mural outdoors.
questions.model: Once dry, acrylic is water-resistant and lasts, so it can handle weather.
questions.why: Durability makes it suitable for outdoors.

questions.q: Where did the Papunya painting movement begin?
questions.why: Papunya is a community in the Northern Territory of Australia.

panel.q: Why do some painters keep a spray bottle for acrylic?
o: To clean the sky in the picture
To change the colours of the paint
To keep paint damp on the palette
panel.why: Misting slows drying.

panel.q: Dry white acrylic is painted over dark blue but still looks bluish. A fix is...
panel.why: Opacity builds with more coats.

panel.q: Compare how you would use acrylic thin like watercolour and thick like oil.
panel.model: Thinned with water it makes see-through washes, while thick straight paint gives bold opaque strokes with texture.
panel.why: Acrylic is flexible.

teach.model: Acrylic paint is water-based and dries fast. When dry, it is water-resistant. You can paint it thin or thick, and layer it. Wash your brushes before the paint hardens.

points.ask: How do I keep brushes safe?

stages.title: Basic sculpture
stages.hook: Walk around a statue in a park or a picture of one. What changes as you move?
explain: Sculpture is art you can walk around. Free-standing sculpture is seen from all sides. Relief sculpture stands out from a flat background, like a coin or a carved panel.

There are four main methods. Carving removes material from a block of stone, wood or ice. Modelling builds up soft material like clay. Casting pours liquid into a mould, such as bronze. Assembling joins found or made parts together.

People have made sculpture for tens of thousands of years. The Moai of Rapa Nui (Easter Island) are huge carved stone figures. Ife heads from Ife in Nigeria were cast from copper alloy and also made in terracotta. In India, temples are decorated with relief carvings. All of these show skill and meaning in 3D.

example.q: Is carving a stone figure an additive or subtractive process?
steps: Carving takes material away.
A process that takes away is subtractive.
Adding is the opposite: modelling clay.
So carving is subtractive.

analogies.home: Cutting a shape out of a bar of soap is carving; building a clay pot is modelling.
analogies.nature: Wind carves rocks over time, a slow natural sculpting.
analogies.city: Statues and fountains in squares are public sculptures.
analogies.farm: A scarecrow assembled from straw and old clothes is assembled sculpture.

stages.mnemonic: Carve it off, model it on, cast it in, assemble the bits.
terms: Cutting material away to reveal a form.
Pouring liquid material into a mould.
Sculpture raised from a flat background.

misc.wrong: Sculpture is only made of stone.
misc.right: Sculpture is made of many materials: clay, wood, metal, ice, paper, found objects.

stages.limits: Dating and attributing ancient sculpture often relies on scholarly estimates.

trip.prompt: Look at the Moai. What process do you think was used to make them?

questions.q: Which method removes material?
questions.why: Carving is subtractive.

questions.q: Which method builds up clay?
questions.why: Modelling adds soft material.

questions.q: What is a relief sculpture?
o: One that floats in the air above a stand
One shown in a museum only
One that rises from a flat background
One that hangs from a rope
questions.why: Relief is attached to a background.

questions.q: How is bronze usually shaped into a sculpture?
questions.why: Metal is melted and poured into a mould.

questions.q: Where are the Moai?
questions.why: The Moai are on Rapa Nui, part of Chile.

questions.q: You make a figure from wire, cardboard and bottle caps. What method is it?
questions.why: Joining parts is assemblage.

questions.q: A sculptor wants a small clay animal and keeps adding bits. What type of process?
questions.why: Adding material is additive.

questions.q: Match the method to the material.
questions.why: Each method suits certain materials.

questions.q: Explain why a sculptor walks around a work in progress.
questions.model: Sculpture is three-dimensional, so it must look good from every side and angle.
questions.why: Viewing from all angles is part of making sculpture.

questions.q: Why is carving harder to correct than modelling?
o: Stone is a soft material, so it breaks easily when carved
You cannot put removed material back easily
Clay is so hard that adding material is difficult
Carving is faster, so there is less time to correct
questions.why: Subtractive methods allow little undoing.

panel.q: Why might sculptors in many places have used stone?
o: It lasts a very long time
It floats on water for easy moving
It is always soft and easy to cut
It is rare everywhere in the world
panel.why: Stone is durable.

panel.q: A work from Ife and the Moai look different. What can be said?
o: Ife heads are better because they are cast in metal alone
Neither counts as art because they served religion
They are the same style because both show a face
Both are great sculpture traditions with different materials and styles
panel.why: Traditions are valued without ranking.

panel.q: Choose one sculpture method and give a material that suits it.
panel.model: Modelling suits clay because it is soft and can be built up.
panel.why: Match method to material.

teach.model: Sculpture is art in three dimensions. You can carve, model, cast or assemble. Carving removes material and modelling adds it. A relief stands out from a flat surface.

points.ask: What ways are there to make sculpture?
What is the difference between carving and modelling?

stages.title: Introduction to art history
stages.hook: If you could visit any time in the past to see art being made, when and where would you go?
explain: Art history is the story of art made by people across time and across the world. It asks who made a work, when, where, with what, and why.

Some very old art comes from caves. In Chauvet Cave in France, paintings are over 30,000 years old. Ancient Egyptians built the Great Pyramid of Giza about 4,500 years ago. Greek builders finished the Parthenon in Athens in the 400s BCE. Leonardo da Vinci painted the Mona Lisa in the early 1500s. The Japanese artist Hokusai made The Great Wave around 1831.

Art history is not one straight line. Great art grew in Africa, Asia, the Americas, Oceania and Europe at the same time, and traditions inspired one another. Museums now try to show many cultures with respect and fairness.

example.q: Which is older: the Parthenon or the Mona Lisa?
steps: The Parthenon was built in the 400s BCE.
The Mona Lisa was painted in the 1500s CE.
BCE comes before CE.
So the Parthenon is older by about 1,900 years.

analogies.home: A family photo album is a small art history of your own family.
analogies.city: Old buildings and new buildings in one street show different times in art.
analogies.music: Songs from different eras show changing styles, like paintings.
analogies.tech: Digital art is a new chapter in the long story of art.

stages.mnemonic: Cave, pyramid, Parthenon, Mona Lisa, Wave: five steps through time.
terms: The study of art through time and place.
Years counted back from year 1; "before the common era".
Ways of making art passed from generation to generation.

misc.wrong: Art history is only about famous European painters.
misc.right: Art history covers every continent and many kinds of art: pottery, textiles, architecture, masks, murals and more.

stages.limits: Many dates for ancient art are estimates by scientists and may be updated.

trip.prompt: Choose a time period on the page. What kinds of art do you find?

questions.q: Put these in order from oldest to newest.
questions.why: About 30,000+ years ago, about 4,500 years ago, 400s BCE, early 1500s, about 1831.

questions.q: Where is Chauvet Cave?
questions.why: Chauvet Cave is in southern France.

questions.q: Who made The Great Wave?
questions.why: Katsushika Hokusai made the print.

questions.q: Where is the Parthenon?
o: Rome, Italy, home of the Colosseum
questions.why: The Parthenon stands on the Acropolis in Athens.

questions.q: About how old is the Great Pyramid of Giza?
questions.why: It was built around 2560 BCE, so about 4,500 years ago.

questions.q: The Mona Lisa was painted around 1503 to 1519. About how many years was it from 1503 to 2003?
What does art history study?
o: Only the prices paid for art
questions.why: It asks who, when, where and why.

questions.q: Which is true about art history?
o: It started in Europe only and spread out
It includes art from every continent
questions.why: Art traditions arose in all places.

questions.q: Explain why dates for very old cave art are given as estimates.
questions.model: Nobody wrote down when it was made, so scientists use tests such as radiocarbon dating and give estimated ages.
questions.why: Prehistoric art was made before written records.

questions.q: A museum shows art only from one place. What is a fair improvement?
o: Remove all the art from the walls
Show fewer works from that place
questions.why: Art history includes many traditions.

panel.q: Why might ancient Egyptian and Greek art look different?
o: One culture was less skilled than the other
Their art looks the same when seen from a distance
They were separate cultures with different ideas
panel.why: Cultures develop their own styles.

panel.q: Why do dates like 400s BCE count down?
o: They are only guesses made by some historians
They are years in the future
BCE years are counted back from year 1
They count up from the year 1 onwards
panel.why: The larger the BCE number, the older.

panel.q: Choose one artwork from this stage and say what it tells us about people of its time.
panel.model: The Great Pyramid shows that ancient Egyptians had skilled builders and strong beliefs about kings and the afterlife.
panel.why: Artworks reveal beliefs and skills.

teach.model: Art history is the story of art across time and the world. There are cave paintings, pyramids, temples, paintings and prints. It includes every continent. Dates for old things are often estimates.
